content: 1. The absolute number of new autochthonous cases detected within a specific population over a defined time period (typically one year) is a critical metric. The ultimate goal in leprosy elimination is achieving zero new autochthonous cases in a given area. This indicator becomes particularly valuable when the number of new cases is very low, as it directly reflects the progress toward elimination. 2. The proportion of new cases born abroad among the total new cases detected is expressed as a percentage. This indicator helps assess the contribution of foreign-born individuals to the overall disease burden. 3. The rate of new cases with grade-2 disability (G2D) is calculated as the number of such cases detected in a specific area during a defined period (typically one year) relative to the population of that area. This rate is expressed per million mid-year population and serves as an important measure of the effectiveness of early detection and treatment efforts. 4. A sporadic autochthonous leprosy case refers to a case that occurs in an area after the disease has been declared eliminated in that region. If two such cases occur within one year, or if cases are reported in two consecutive years post-elimination, they are considered clustered, and the area’s status reverts to pre-elimination. However, if the cases are determined to be unrelated, they remain classified as sporadic, and the elimination status of the area is maintained. 5. Dr. VRR Pemmaraju outlined the phases on the pathway to leprosy elimination. A matrix was developed to describe the definitions, milestones, criteria, and indicators for assessing progress toward transmission interruption and disease elimination. This matrix is intended to assist countries in preparing dossiers for WHO verification of elimination. The four phases in the journey toward elimination are: Phase 1: Until elimination as a public health problem. Phase 2: Until transmission interruption. Phase 3: Until disease elimination. Phase 4: Post-elimination surveillance. 6. For each phase, programs must meet specific criteria and ensure the availability of necessary facilities and interventions. Indicators and cut-off levels in the matrix will measure progress toward elimination. As most countries have achieved elimination as a public health problem, discussions now focus on transmission interruption, disease elimination, and post-elimination surveillance. 7. Political commitment is essential for the successful implementation of national programs. This includes the presence of a country-owned national strategic plan aligned with the Global Leprosy Strategy 2021–2030 and the NTD Roadmap 2021–2030. Budget allocation and operational funding are also indicators of commitment. Political commitment must be assessed across all phases, from transmission interruption to post-elimination. 8. The allocation of dedicated staff and capacity building for healthcare workers is crucial for providing quality leprosy services. Adequate numbers of trained staff at the operational level are necessary for program implementation, particularly during the transition from transmission interruption to post-elimination. Training programs, whether specific to leprosy or integrated with other disease control programs, will be evaluated. 9. Raising awareness about leprosy among the general population and healthcare workers is vital for early detection and prompt treatment with multidrug therapy (MDT). Awareness campaigns are linked to improved community response and early case detection. However, this is a lower priority in countries where leprosy is primarily seen among foreign-born individuals or in the post-elimination phase. 10. Advocacy with policymakers is necessary to secure political support for leprosy elimination and sustained surveillance in the post-elimination phase. Regular communication with policymakers through meetings, briefings, and status reports is recommended. Verifiable indicators include meeting minutes, published reports, and brochures. 11. Organized partnerships at national and sub-national levels are important for coordinated efforts in leprosy elimination. These partnerships help prevent duplication of interventions and ensure effective implementation. The presence of such partnerships will be evaluated as part of the elimination process. 12. Sustaining leprosy interventions, including early detection, diagnosis, and MDT treatment for new cases and relapses, is essential for transmission interruption and disease elimination. The evaluation will assess the availability and accessibility of these services, trends in leprosy among women and children, and the capacity to detect relapses. 13. Prevention and management of complications, such as reactions and disabilities, are critical components of quality leprosy services. Evaluations will review the availability of skilled staff, infrastructure, and counseling services. Indicators include the number of patients receiving management services for complications. 14. Effective surveillance and improved data management systems are essential for evaluating leprosy programs. A sensitive surveillance system detects cases before disabilities develop. In low-endemic countries, the presence of an effective system to detect all cases will be verified. Post-elimination surveillance should be maintained for at least ten years to identify sporadic cases. 15. Contact tracing is emphasized as a mandatory intervention in both highand low-endemic settings. Contacts of leprosy patients have a higher risk of infection. Evaluations will review the routine implementation of contact screening and its coverage. 16. Post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) with single-dose rifampicin (SDR) is recommended as a strategic direction in the Global Leprosy Strategy 2021–2030. In countries adopting PEP, evaluations will assess the coverage of contacts provided with SDR and the number of new cases detected during chemoprophylaxis activities. 17. National programs are encouraged to map areas that have achieved transmission interruption or disease elimination. Internal evaluations should document that sub-national units meet all criteria for transmission interruption. Evaluation reports from sub-national units will be presented to external teams verifying national disease elimination. 18. Countries that have not reported a single autochthonous case for more than ten consecutive years may submit a declaration to demonstrate leprosy elimination at the national level.
